aliases: shingle basket;making of shingle baskets from pulled shingles

label: Clubrush Work of Kruunupyy
defn: Weaving of clubrush (bulrush) into mats and objects in Kruunupyy (Kronoby), Finland.

label: Himmeli
defn: Geometric hanging mobiles of straw tubes threaded together, made at Christmas in Finland and the Baltic (Lithuanian sodai).

label: Straw Weaving in Belarus
defn: Belarusian straw weaving of ritual and decorative objects — figures, baskets, spiders (paŭki) and boxes (UNESCO 2025).

label: Turiisk Straw Plaiting
defn: Straw plaiting tradition of Turiisk hromada in Volyn Oblast (Ukraine).

label: Iza Vine Weaving
defn: Willow-vine basket and furniture weaving of the village of Iza in Zakarpattia (Ukraine).

label: Shchitky Reed Weaving
defn: Reed weaving tradition of Shchitky and Pysarivka (Vinnytsia Oblast, Ukraine).

label: Wayuu Weaving
defn: the crocheted and loom-woven fibre work of Wayuu women of the Guajira Peninsula (Colombia and Venezuela), with named geometric kanaas designs: mochila (susu) bags, chinchorro hammocks.
aliases: Wayuu mochila; susu; tejido wayuu; kanaas

label: Kiondo
defn: twined bags of sisal and other vegetable twine with leather trim made by Kikuyu, Kamba and Taita women of Kenya, patterned in dyed bands.

label: Skep
defn: coiled-straw (earlier wicker) beehives sewn with bramble strips by skeppers of northern and western Europe and the British Isles, from the Middle Ages: straw skeps, skep caps.

label: Nantucket Lightship Baskets
defn: rattan-and-cane baskets woven over wooden moulds with solid turned bases, first by keepers of the Nantucket lightships in the 19th century, later lidded purses with carved ivory and scrimshaw.

label: Zulu Beadwork
defn: Glass-bead regalia of the Zulu of KwaZulu-Natal in brick stitch, with colour codes by region and age: ucu necklaces, love-letter panels (incwadi), beaded aprons and skirts.

label: Maasai Beadwork
defn: Beaded collars, earrings and headdresses of the Maasai of Kenya and Tanzania: flat disc collars, wedding necklaces.

label: Yoruba Beadwork
defn: Beaded regalia of Yoruba kings and Ifa priests: beaded crowns with veils (ade), diviners' bags, beaded staffs.

label: Mexican Featherwork
defn: Feather mosaic of Mesoamerica and colonial New Spain (amanteca), from Aztec shields and headdresses to Christian feather paintings: Moctezuma's headdress, Mass of Saint Gregory (1539).

label: Porcupine Quillwork
defn: Embroidery with flattened dyed porcupine quills on hide and birchbark across the Plains, Subarctic and Northeast: Lakota quilled robes and shirts, Mi'kmaq and Odawa quilled birchbark boxes, Dene quilled bands.

label: Plains Beadwork
defn: Glass-bead embroidery of the peoples of the Great Plains and Plateau in lane-stitch and overlay techniques, in tribal styles: Lakota fully beaded vests and cradleboards, Crow (Apsáalooke) horse gear, Blackfeet and Cree floral beadwork.

label: Haudenosaunee Raised Beadwork
defn: Raised (embossed) glass beadwork on velvet by Mohawk, Tuscarora and Seneca women, above all the 'whimsies' (pincushions, frames, purses) sold at Niagara Falls from the mid-19th century.

label: Wampum
defn: Tubular beads of white whelk and purple quahog shell strung and woven into belts and strings by the Haudenosaunee and Algonquian peoples of the Northeast to record treaties and council business: Hiawatha Belt, Two Row Wampum.

label: Hawaiian Featherwork
defn: The featherwork of the Hawaiian chiefs: red and yellow honeyeater and ʻiʻiwi feathers knotted to olonā netting as emblems of rank and divinity: ʻahu ʻula cloaks and capes, mahiole helmets, lei hulu, feathered god images.

label: Kahu Huruhuru
defn: Māori feather cloaks: muka cloaks finger-woven (whatu) with feathers of kiwi, kererū, kākā and other birds set in the weft, the highest-ranking cloaks of the 19th century onward: kahu kiwi, kahu kererū.

label: Jutti
defn: embroidered leather slip-on shoes of Punjab with straight lasts and upturned toes, worked in silk, gold and silver thread (tilla): tilla jutti, Patiala jutti, mojari, khussa.
aliases: Punjabi jutti; mojari; khussa; tilla jutti

label: Western Leatherwork
defn: the tooled, carved and silver-mounted leather of the vaquero and cowboy tradition, from Iberia and New Spain to the American West, Hawaii and the Great Basin: vaquero saddles, Sheridan-style floral carving, buckaroo gear, cowboy boots.
aliases: vaquero saddlery; Western saddlery; Western leather carving

label: Moroccan Leatherwork
defn: vegetable-tanned leather of Fez and Marrakech cut, stitched and embroidered in silk and metal thread on poufs, slippers and bags: embroidered poufs, babouches.

label: Mashrabiya
defn: screens of turned wooden spindles in latticework, for windows and balconies of Cairo and the Arab world.

label: Khatam
defn: Persian micro-marquetry of wood, bone and metal assembled in geometric patterns (Shiraz, Isfahan).

label: Ottoman Mother-of-Pearl Inlay
defn: Ottoman woodwork inlaid with mother-of-pearl, tortoiseshell and ivory (sedefkârlık): Qur'an stands, chests and thrones.

label: Palestinian Olive-Wood Carving
defn: carved olive wood of Bethlehem and Jerusalem, devotional and souvenir objects since the 16th century.

label: Islamic Woodwork
defn: carved and joined woodwork of the Islamic world outside the named leaves: minbars, Qur'an stands and cenotaphs carved in bevelled and geometric strapwork (the Minbar of Nur al-Din, Aleppo 1168).

label: ʿAjami
defn: painted, gessoed and gilded wooden panelling of Ottoman Syrian reception rooms (the Aleppo Room, 1600–03; the Damascus Room, 1707).

label: Kondapalli Toys
defn: Carved and painted softwood (tella poniki) figures of Kondapalli in Andhra Pradesh: Dasavatara sets, ambari elephant.

label: Nirmal Toys
defn: Painted softwood toys and lacquered paintings of the Naqqash families of Nirmal in Telangana.

label: Malay Woodcarving
defn: The carved wood of the Malay Peninsula, above all of Kelantan and Terengganu, for palaces, houses, boats and weapon hilts, in pierced floral (awan larat) designs.

label: Yosegi-zaiku
defn: Wood mosaic of Hakone: blocks of differently coloured woods glued into patterns and planed into veneers for boxes and puzzle boxes.

label: Ainu Woodcarving
defn: Ainu carving of wood in curving and scale designs: prayer sticks (ikupasuy), trays, knife hilts (makiri) and ritual objects, and the carved trays of Nibutani.

label: Hwagak
defn: Korean painted ox-horn veneer: thin translucent horn sheets painted on the back in bright colours and laid on boxes and furniture; makers designated hwagakjang.

label: Mate Burilado
defn: Engraved and pyrographed gourds of the central Peruvian Andes (Huanta, Cochas Chico), with dense narrative scenes.

label: Bentwood Boxes
defn: Kerfed, steamed and bent cedar boxes and chests of the Northwest Coast, carved and painted in formline: storage and grease boxes, bentwood chests, bent-corner bowls.

label: Fijian Clubs
defn: The carved hardwood war clubs (i-wau) of Fiji, made by specialist carvers in named forms and often finely incised: totokia (pineapple club), gata (gunstock club), i-ula throwing clubs, kinikini paddle clubs.

label: Tramp Art
defn: American and European woodwork of c. 1870–1940 built up from notch-carved layers of cigar-box and crate wood: boxes, frames, miniature furniture.

label: Abramtsevo-Kudrino Carving
defn: Flat relief wood carving of curling floral ornament on boxes, ladles and furniture, created at the Abramtsevo estate workshop by Vasily Vornoskov of Kudrino (late 19th century) and continued at Khotkovo.

label: Untsukul Inlay
defn: Woodwork of the Avar village of Untsukul (Dagestan) inlaid with fine silver and cupronickel wire and plates in geometric patterns: walking sticks, boxes, vases.

label: Hutsul Wood Carving
defn: Carving and inlay of the Hutsuls of the Ukrainian Carpathians — chip carving, beadwork inlay and brass inlay on boxes, plates and crosses (Shkriblyak family).

label: Chernihiv Wood Carving
defn: Traditional artistic wood carving of Chernihiv Oblast (Ukraine).
aliases: artistic wood carving of Chernihiv Oblast

label: Konjic Woodcarving
defn: Woodcarving of Konjic in Bosnia and Herzegovina, with dense floral and geometric relief on furniture and interiors (UNESCO 2017).

label: Kuksa
defn: Carved drinking cups of birch burl made by the Sámi and Finns.

label: Boulle Work
defn: Marquetry of tortoiseshell and brass (with pewter and horn) cut together in première- and contre-partie sheets, perfected for Louis XIV's court by André-Charles Boulle and revived in the 19th century: Boulle commodes for the Trianon, bracket clocks and pedestals, bureaux plats.

label: Essaouira Thuya Marquetry
defn: inlay and marquetry in thuya burl of the workshops of Essaouira in Morocco, with lemonwood, ebony and mother-of-pearl tapped flush into the burl: boxes, trays, panels.

label: Kashmir Walnut Wood Carving
defn: deep relief, undercut and openwork carving in walnut of Kashmir, with chinar leaf, lotus and vine designs on furniture, screens and boxes (GI 2008).
aliases: Kashmiri woodcarving; walnut wood carving of Kashmir

label: Jepara Wood Carving
defn: relief and pierced carving in teak of Jepara in Central Java, from the 16th-century panels of the Mantingan Mosque to carved furniture and screens.

label: Magewappa
defn: steam-bent boxes of straight-grained Akita cedar from Ōdate, stitched with cherry bark, made since the Edo period (designated traditional craft 1980).

label: Tendō Shōgi Koma
defn: shogi pieces of Tendō in Yamagata, written, carved or raised in lacquer in named calligraphic styles since the late Edo period (traditional craft 1996).

label: Vardo
defn: the horse-drawn living wagons of British Romani Travellers from c. 1870, carved, painted with scrollwork and gilded, in named types: Reading, ledge, bow-top, Burton wagons.
aliases: Romani wagon; Gypsy caravan; vardo painting

label: Danish Freehand Pipes
defn: free-form briar pipes carved to the grain, from Sixten Ivarsson's Copenhagen workshop in the 1950s and his pupils (Jess Chonowitsch, Lars Ivarsson).

label: Persian Lacquer
defn: painted and varnished papier-mâché and wood of Iran — pen boxes, mirror cases, bindings and caskets — from the Timurid and Safavid periods to its Zand and Qajar flowering (Muhammad Zaman, 'Ali Ashraf, Muhammad Isma'il).

label: Kashmiri Papier-Mâché
defn: painted and varnished papier-mâché of Kashmir (boxes, vases), with floral and hunting designs.

label: Edirnekâri
defn: Ottoman lacquer of Edirne (17th–19th century): writing boxes, bookbindings and furniture painted with flowers under varnish.

label: Channapatna Toys
defn: Lathe-turned wooden toys of Channapatna in Karnataka finished in coloured lac.

label: Etikoppaka Toys
defn: Lac-turned wooden toys of Etikoppaka in Andhra Pradesh coloured with vegetable dyes.

label: Burmese Lacquerware
defn: Coiled-bamboo and horsehair vessels coated in thitsi lacquer, engraved (yun) or gilded and glass-inlaid, made above all in Bagan: offering vessels (hsun-ok), betel boxes, manuscript chests.

label: Lai Rot Nam
defn: Thai gold-and-black lacquer decoration on wood, made by gold leaf on a lacquer ground with a water-washed resist: manuscript cabinets, temple doors and window shutters.

label: Carved Lacquer
defn: Chinese lacquer built up in many layers and carved in relief, from the Song: tihong cinnabar lacquer, tixi guri scrolls, Yongle and Qianlong imperial boxes.

label: Maki-e
defn: Japanese lacquer decorated with sprinkled gold and silver powder, from the Heian period: Kōdaiji maki-e, Hon'ami Kōetsu's writing boxes, inrō, Nanban export lacquer.

label: Japanese Lacquerware
defn: Japanese lacquer other than maki-e, made in regional centres named for their wares: Wajima-nuri, Tsugaru-nuri, Kamakura-bori, Negoro, and raden mother-of-pearl inlay.

label: Ryukyuan Lacquerware
defn: Lacquer of the Ryukyu kingdom (15th–19th century) with red grounds, mother-of-pearl inlay, gold-leaf (chinkin) and relief (tsuikin) decoration.

label: Najeonchilgi
defn: Korean lacquer inlaid with mother-of-pearl, from Goryeo sutra boxes to Joseon clothing chests; makers designated najeonjang and chiljang.

label: Yi Lacquerware
defn: Red, yellow and black painted lacquer of the Yi (Nuosu) of Liangshan in Sichuan: wooden bowls, cups and armour.

label: Kintsugi
defn: Japanese repair of broken ceramics with lacquer dusted with gold, valued as an aesthetic in its own right since the 16th century.

label: Mexican Lacquerware
defn: Lacquer (maque) of Mexico made with insect and seed-oil lacquers on gourds and wood, by inlay or painting, in its regional centres: Olinalá boxes, Pátzcuaro gilded trays, Chiapa de Corzo gourds.

label: Barniz de Pasto
defn: Decoration of wood with sheets of mopa-mopa resin cut and applied in colour, practised in Pasto (Nariño) since the colonial period (UNESCO urgent safeguarding 2020).

label: Khokhloma
defn: Painted and varnished turned woodenware of the Nizhny Novgorod region (Semyonov, Khokhloma) since the 17th century, with red and black foliage over a gold-like ground produced by tin powder and oven-hardened varnish: bowls, spoons, ladles.

label: Palekh Miniature
defn: Lacquer miniature painting in egg tempera on black papier-mâché boxes from Palekh, created by former icon painters in 1923 (Golikov), with fairy-tale scenes in gold.

label: Fedoskino Miniature
defn: Lacquer miniature painting in oils on papier-mâché from Fedoskino near Moscow since 1795 (Lukutin factory), with genre scenes over mother-of-pearl and metal-leaf grounds.

label: Mstyora Miniature
defn: Lacquer miniature painting of Mstyora (Vladimir region) from 1923, with landscapes in warm tones and gold ornament on papier-mâché.

label: Kholuy Miniature
defn: Lacquer miniature painting of Kholuy (Ivanovo region) from 1934, by former icon painters, with dense narrative scenes in blue and green.

label: Soban
defn: Korean small portable dining tables of wood in regional styles (Naju, Haeju, Tongyeong); makers designated sobanjang.

label: Queen Anne Style (furniture)
defn: English and American furniture of c. 1700–1755 with cabriole legs, pad and claw-and-ball feet, shell carving and walnut veneers, continuing in the colonies after Queen Anne's reign: Philadelphia and Newport high chests, vase-splat side chairs, bonnet-top highboys.
aliases: Queen Anne furniture;Queen Anne style furniture

label: Chippendale Furniture
defn: English and American furniture of c. 1750–1790 after Thomas Chippendale's pattern book The Gentleman and Cabinet-Maker's Director (1754), in Rococo, Gothic and Chinese taste in mahogany: Director plates, ribbon-back chairs, Philadelphia Chippendale high chests, Newport block-front desks.

label: Hepplewhite Style
defn: English and American Neoclassical furniture of c. 1775–1800 after George Hepplewhite's Cabinet-Maker and Upholsterer's Guide (1788): shield- and heart-back chairs, square tapering legs, inlaid satinwood: shield-back chairs, Federal sideboards with spade feet.

label: Sheraton Style
defn: English and American late Neoclassical furniture of c. 1790–1820 after Thomas Sheraton's Cabinet-Maker and Upholsterer's Drawing-Book (1791–94): straight lines, turned and reeded legs, painted and inlaid satinwood: Drawing-Book designs, square-back chairs, Duncan Phyfe's early work.

label: International Gothic (decorative arts)
defn: Courtly late Gothic goldsmiths' work, tapestry and glass (c. 1250–1450): the Goldenes Rössl, the Apocalypse Tapestry of Angers.

label: Mannerism (decorative arts)
defn: Renaissance and Mannerist decorative arts and ornament (c. 1450–1600): Cellini's Salt Cellar, Jamnitzer's goldsmiths' work, Pannemaker's tapestries.

label: Louis XIV Style
defn: French court decorative arts c. 1660–1715 under Le Brun: Boulle marquetry, Gobelins tapestries, Versailles silver furniture.

label: Louis XV Style
defn: The Rococo decorative arts of France c. 1715–1760: Cressent's commodes, Meissonnier's ornament, Vincennes-Sèvres porcelain.

label: Louis XVI Style
defn: Early neoclassical decorative arts in France c. 1760–1790: Riesener's furniture, Marie-Antoinette's boudoir at Fontainebleau.

label: Empire Style
defn: Napoleonic neoclassical design c. 1800–1830: Percier and Fontaine's Malmaison, Jacob-Desmalter's furniture.

label: Biedermeier
defn: Central European design and domestic culture 1815–1848, simple and comfortable, and its painting of bourgeois life: Danhauser furniture, Waldmüller's genre scenes.

label: Victorian Decorative Arts
defn: British decorative arts 1837–1901, historicist and industrial: Pugin's Gothic Revival furniture, Minton majolica.

label: Arts and Crafts Movement
defn: The reform of design and craft after Ruskin and Morris (1860s–1920s): Morris & Co. wallpapers, Ashbee's silver, Stickley's Craftsman furniture.

label: Art Nouveau
defn: The international style of organic line and ornament c. 1890–1910 across design, architecture and painting: Gallé's glass, Mucha's posters, Horta's Hôtel Tassel, Klimt's Beethoven Frieze.

label: Art Deco
defn: The streamlined geometric luxury style of the 1920s–1930s: Ruhlmann's furniture, Lalique glass, Cassandre's posters, the Chrysler Building.

label: Mingei
defn: The Japanese folk-craft movement (1926) of Yanagi Sōetsu, Hamada and Kawai: Hamada Shōji's stoneware, Serizawa Keisuke's stencil dyeing.

label: Mid-Century Modern
defn: Designer-makers born c. 1910–1944 outside the design schools of N Design: craft furniture makers, studio ceramists, fibre artists, art jewellers, fashion and costume designers. Serial-production designers now sit in N Design leaves.

label: Contemporary Design
defn: Designer-makers born from 1945 outside the design schools of N Design: craft furniture, studio ceramics, fibre art, art jewellery, fashion and costume design. Serial-production designers now sit in N Design leaves.

label: Bezalel School
defn: the style of the Bezalel School of Arts and Crafts in Jerusalem (from 1906), founded by Boris Schatz to create a Jewish national art, its workshops of Yemenite Jewish silversmiths making filigree Judaica: Hanukkah lamps, Torah ornaments, spice boxes, Bezalel carpets.
aliases: Bezalel style; Bezalel School of Arts and Crafts

label: Shaker Furniture
defn: the plain, finely made furniture of the Shaker communities of New England, New York and Kentucky in the 19th century: ladder-back and rocking chairs, trestle tables, peg rails, oval boxes.

label: Chinese Classical Furniture
defn: hardwood furniture of China in huanghuali, zitan and other woods, joined without glue or nails, plain under the Ming and heavier and carved under the Qing: painting tables, horseshoe armchairs, recessed-leg tables.
aliases: Ming furniture; Ming and Qing hardwood furniture; huanghuali furniture

label: Tansu
defn: Japanese mobile chests of the Edo and Meiji periods with forged iron hardware and lacquer finishes, in regional and functional types: isho-dansu, kaidan-dansu, funa-dansu, Sendai tansu.

label: Bandaji
defn: Korean drop-front storage chests of the Joseon period, read by region from their cut-metal fittings: Ganghwa, Kaesong and Namhansanseong bandaji.

label: Vanuatu Slit Gongs
defn: The upright slit gongs of northern Vanuatu (Ambrym, Malakula), breadfruit trunks hollowed and carved with ancestral faces and raised in dancing grounds of the grade societies: atingting kon (Ambrym), Malakula slit gongs; tree-fern grade figures as a kind.

label: Spanish Guitar
defn: the classical and flamenco guitar as built by the Spanish workshops of Seville, Almería and Madrid from Antonio de Torres (19th century) and the Ramírez dynasty.
aliases: classical guitar making; guitarra española; flamenco guitar

label: Djembe
defn: goblet drums carved from a single log by Mande smiths (numu) of West Africa, rope-tuned, often with carved bases.

label: Mbira
defn: lamellophones of the Shona of Zimbabwe with forged keys on a hardwood soundboard set in a calabash resonator (UNESCO 2020): mbira dzavadzimu, nyunga nyunga.

label: Violin Making
defn: the European lutherie of the violin family, in named schools and centres from 16th-century Cremona (Amati, Stradivari, Guarneri; UNESCO 2012) to Mittenwald, Mirecourt and the Vogtland.
aliases: lutherie; Cremonese violin making; violin craftsmanship

label: Tanpura
defn: the long-necked drone lute of Indian classical music with a gourd resonator, made above all by the family workshops of Miraj since c. 1850, with the sitar.
aliases: tambura; Miraj tanpura; Miraj instrument making

label: Saraswati Veena
defn: the 24-fret veena of Carnatic music with a resonator hollowed from jackwood, carved and painted, made in Thanjavur since the Nayak court (17th century; GI 2013).

label: Celtic Harp
defn: the harps of Gaelic Ireland, Scotland and Wales, from the carved willow wire-strung clàrsach (Trinity College, Queen Mary and Lamont harps) to the Welsh triple harp.
aliases: clàrsach; cláirseach; Gaelic harp; wire-strung harp

label: Cimbalom
defn: the Central European hammered dulcimer, from folk instruments to József Schunda's concert cimbalom of 1874.

label: Santur
defn: the hammered box zither of Persian and Iraqi maqam music, often decorated with khatam inlay, borrowed into Hindustani music as the santoor.

label: Appalachian Dulcimer
defn: the fretted box zither of Scotch-Irish Appalachia from the early 19th century, with heart and scroll soundholes, revived from the 1950s.

label: Kantele
defn: the Finnish and Karelian plucked psaltery, carved from one piece and later built up, a national symbol tied to the Kalevala.

label: Koto
defn: the Japanese long zither of paulownia with movable bridges, from the court gakusō to the Edo koto of Yatsuhashi Kengyō, often decorated in maki-e.

label: Guzheng
defn: the Chinese long zither with movable bridges, in northern (Shandong, Henan) and southern (Chaozhou, Hakka, Zhejiang) schools.

label: Erhu
defn: the two-string Chinese fiddle (huqin) with hardwood neck and python-skin sound box, made in Beijing, Shanghai and Suzhou.

label: Taus and Dilruba
defn: the bowed fretted lutes of Sikh gurmat music, the taus carved in the form of a peacock, from the 17th century.

label: Sarangi
defn: the bowed fiddle of Hindustani music carved from one block of tun wood, with gut and sympathetic strings.

label: Hardanger Fiddle
defn: the Norwegian fiddle with sympathetic strings, decorated with ink rosing, bone and mother-of-pearl inlay and carved heads, from 1651.

label: Nyckelharpa
defn: the Swedish keyed fiddle of Uppland, from the medieval moraharpa to the chromatic nyckelharpa of the 20th-century revival.

label: Accordion
defn: free-reed bellows instruments with decorated cases, from the Castelfidardo workshops founded by Paolo Soprani (1863) to the Saxon concertina and bandoneon.

label: Bagpipes
defn: bagpipes of the British Isles with turned bores and ivory, silver and horn mounts: Irish uilleann pipes, Great Highland bagpipe.
aliases: uilleann pipes; Highland pipes; piob mhór

label: Gagaku Instruments
defn: the instruments of the Japanese court music, from the Shōsōin lutes and harps to the hichiriki, ryūteki and shō made today.

label: Mechanical Musical Instruments
defn: self-playing instruments in decorated cases and façades: Swiss cylinder music boxes of Geneva and Sainte-Croix, Dutch street organs.
aliases: mechanical music; music boxes; Swiss music-box making

label: Modernist Photography
defn: The period style of photographers born c. 1860–1944 working in the modern idioms of the 20th century outside a recorded school: sharp-focus, experimental and illustrated-press photography between Pictorialism and the contemporary generation: Stieglitz's The Steerage, Kertész's Fork, Sudek's Prague v

label: Street Photography
defn: Candid photography of chance encounters in public places, mostly with the hand-held camera, from 1930s Paris and New York to the 1960s American and Japanese street: Levitt's children's chalk drawings, Frank's The Americans, Winogrand's Women Are Beautiful, Moriyama's Stray Dog.

label: Photojournalism
defn: Photography made to report news for the illustrated press, from the Weimar picture magazines and Life to war and agency photography: Capa's Falling Soldier, Rosenthal's Raising the Flag on Iwo Jima, Eddie Adams's Saigon Execution, Nick Ut's The Terror of War.

label: Surrealist Photography
defn: Photography of the Surrealist movement and its circles, 1920s–1950s, using rayographs, solarisation, staged mannequins and found street images: Man Ray's Rayographs, Boiffard's Big Toe, Bellmer's La Poupée, Grete Stern's Sueños.

label: Fashion Photography
defn: Photography of clothing and models for fashion magazines and advertising, from de Meyer and Steichen at Vogue to the Avedon–Penn generation and the 1960s London and Paris photographers: Steichen's Art of the Gown (1911), Horst's Mainbocher Corset, Avedon's Dovima with Elephants, Penn's Harlequin Dre

label: Düsseldorf School of Photography
defn: The students of Bernd and Hilla Becher at the Kunstakademie Düsseldorf from 1976, making serial, frontal and large-format colour photographs: the Bechers' Water Towers typologies, Gursky's 99 Cent, Struth's Museum Photographs, Ruff's Portraits.

label: Early Photography
defn: Photography of the daguerreotype, calotype, wet-collodion and albumen decades (1839–c. 1880), from the inventors to the survey, war and studio photographers: Talbot's The Open Door, Nadar's portraits, Cameron's portraits.

label: Pictorialism
defn: The first international art-photography movement (1880s–1920s), soft-focus and hand-worked, organised in salons and societies (the Linked Ring, Photo-Club de Paris, Vienna Camera Club, Photo-Secession), together with the other photographers of that generation: Steichen's The Pond—Moonlight, Käsebier

label: Straight Photography
defn: Sharp-focus, unmanipulated modernist photography from the 1910s to the 1950s and the photographers of that generation (born c. 1880–1919) not placed in a named school: Strand's Wall Street, Weston's Pepper No. 30, Adams's Moonrise, Hernandez.

label: New Vision
defn: The experimental photography of the 1920s–1930s (Neues Sehen) of angles, close-ups and photograms: Moholy-Nagy's photograms, Rodchenko's Pioneer Girl.

label: Humanistic Photography
defn: French post-war photography of everyday life and its dignity: Doisneau's Kiss by the Hôtel de Ville, Willy Ronis's Le Petit Parisien.

label: Documentary Photography
defn: Photography that records people, places and events for social or historical purpose, from Riis and Hine to the FSA and the postwar documentary groups, with the other photographers born c. 1920–1944: Lange's Migrant Mother, Evans's Let Us Now Praise Famous Men, Salgado's Gold Mine.

label: Contemporary Photography
defn: Photography by artists born from 1945, staged, documentary and conceptual, sectioned by the named schools (New Topographics, Pictures Generation, Vancouver, Boston and Helsinki Schools) and then by country.

label: Photo-Secession
defn: Members and fellows of the Photo-Secession, the American pictorialist society founded by Alfred Stieglitz in New York in 1902 and shown at the Little Galleries (291) and in Camera Work: Stieglitz, Käsebier, White, Steichen, Coburn, Brigman.

label: Group f/64
defn: Members and exhibitors of Group f/64 (San Francisco, 1932–1935), who championed sharp-focus, full-tonal straight photography against pictorialism: Ansel Adams, Edward Weston, Imogen Cunningham, Willard Van Dyke.

label: Photo League
defn: Members of the Photo League, the New York cooperative of documentary and street photographers (1936–1951), with its Feature Group projects such as Harlem Document: Sol Libsohn, Aaron Siskind, Walter Rosenblum, Ruth Orkin.

label: Magnum Photos
defn: Members, associates and nominees of Magnum Photos, the photographers' cooperative founded in 1947 by Robert Capa, Henri Cartier-Bresson, David Seymour, George Rodger and William Vandivert, the standard-bearer of concerned photography and photo-essay reportage.

label: Umayyad Architecture
defn: the architecture of the Umayyad caliphate (661–750): the Dome of the Rock, the Great Mosque of Damascus and the desert palaces (Qusayr 'Amra, Khirbat al-Mafjar, Mshatta).

label: Abbasid Architecture
defn: the architecture of the Abbasid caliphate (750–1258): Samarra's mosques and palaces, the round city of Baghdad and the Tulunid mosque of Cairo.

label: Fatimid Architecture
defn: the architecture of the Fatimid caliphate in Ifriqiya and Egypt (909–1171): al-Azhar, al-Hakim and the gates of Cairo.

label: Moorish Architecture
defn: the Islamic architecture of al-Andalus and the Maghreb: the caliphal Great Mosque of Córdoba and Madinat al-Zahra, the taifa Aljafería, Almoravid and Almohad mosques and the Nasrid Alhambra.

label: Mudéjar Architecture
defn: the Islamic-derived architecture built under Christian rule in Iberia (12th–16th century), in brick, tile and carpentry (artesonado ceilings).

label: Seljuk Architecture
defn: the architecture of the Great Seljuqs in Iran and Central Asia (11th–12th century): four-iwan mosques, domed chambers, brick tomb towers and minarets.

label: Anatolian Seljuk Architecture
defn: the architecture of the Seljuqs of Rum and the beyliks in Anatolia (12th–14th century): caravanserais, madrasas with carved stone portals, and tomb towers.

label: Mamluk Architecture
defn: the architecture of the Mamluk sultanate in Egypt and Syria (1250–1517): funerary complexes with domes and minarets, ablaq masonry and carved stone domes.

label: Ilkhanid Architecture
defn: the architecture of the Mongol Ilkhanate in Iran (1256–1335): the Mausoleum of Öljeitü at Soltaniyeh and great mosques with tiled portals.

label: Timurid Architecture
defn: the architecture of Timur and his successors in Central Asia and Iran (1370–1507): Samarkand, Herat and Mashhad, with bulbous ribbed domes and tile-mosaic revetment.

label: Safavid Architecture
defn: the architecture of Safavid Iran (1501–1736), above all Isfahan's Naqsh-e Jahan square, its mosques, palaces and bridges.

label: Ottoman Architecture
defn: the architecture of the Ottoman empire from the early Bursa and Edirne mosques through the classical domed mosques of Mimar Sinan to Ottoman Baroque.

label: Qajar Architecture
defn: the architecture of Qajar Iran (1789–1925): palaces and mosques with polychrome figural tiles (Golestan Palace).

label: Indo-Islamic Architecture
defn: the Islamic architecture of the South Asian sultanates before and beside the Mughals: Delhi Sultanate (Qutb Minar), Gujarat, Bengal, Malwa and the Deccan sultanates.

label: Mughal Architecture
defn: the architecture of the Mughal empire (1526–1857): Humayun's tomb, Fatehpur Sikri, the Taj Mahal and the Mughal gardens.

label: Sudano-Sahelian Architecture
defn: the earthen architecture of the West African Sahel: mud-brick mosques with projecting torons (Djenné, Timbuktu, Agadez).

label: Swahili Architecture
defn: the coral-stone architecture of the Swahili coast (Kilwa, Lamu, Zanzibar): mosques, pillar tombs and carved doors.

label: Chinese Islamic Architecture
defn: mosques of China in the Chinese timber-frame idiom (Xi'an, Niujie) and the brick and tiled mosques of Xinjiang.

label: Javanese Mosque Architecture
defn: the mosques of Java and the Malay world built in the regional timber idiom with stacked pyramidal (tajug) roofs instead of domes (Demak, Kudus, Menara Kudus).

label: Moorish Revival Architecture
defn: the 19th–20th-century revival of Moorish and Islamic forms in Europe and the Americas — synagogues, theatres, baths and palaces.

label: Neo-Mudéjar
defn: the Spanish revival of Mudéjar brick and tile (late 19th–early 20th century): bullrings, stations and schools.

label: Neo-Mamluk Architecture
defn: the revival of Mamluk forms in Egypt and beyond (late 19th–20th century).

label: First National Architectural Movement
defn: the Turkish national style of 1908–1930 reviving Ottoman and Seljuq forms (Vedat Tek, Mimar Kemaleddin).

label: Indo-Saracenic Architecture
defn: the British colonial revival style in India (from the 1870s) combining Indo-Islamic and Mughal forms with Gothic and Neoclassical planning: railway stations, courts and palaces (Robert Fellowes Chisholm, Charles Mant).

label: Gothic Revival Architecture
defn: The revival of medieval Gothic forms from the mid-18th century to the early 20th, in churches, colleges, parliaments and houses: the Palace of Westminster, Cologne Cathedral's completion, St Patrick's Cathedral, New York.

label: Tudor Revival Architecture
defn: The revival of Tudor and Elizabethan domestic forms (half-timbering, tall chimneys, mullioned windows) in late 19th- and 20th-century houses: Jacobethan country houses, mock-Tudor suburban villas.

label: Romanesque Revival Architecture
defn: The 19th-century revival of round-arched Romanesque forms, from the German Rundbogenstil to Richardsonian Romanesque in America: Trinity Church, Boston, the Natural History Museum, London.

label: Neo-Byzantine Architecture
defn: The 19th–20th-century revival of Byzantine domes, arcades and banded masonry, in Orthodox and Catholic churches and public buildings: Sacré-Cœur, Paris, Westminster Cathedral, Saint Sava, Belgrade.

label: Renaissance Revival Architecture
defn: The 19th-century revival of Italian, French and Northern Renaissance forms for palaces, banks, museums and civic buildings: the Vienna State Opera, the Reform Club, the Rijksmuseum.

label: Italianate Architecture
defn: The 19th-century picturesque revival of Italian villa and palazzo forms, with bracketed eaves and towers, popular in Britain and North America: Osborne House, Italianate row houses of San Francisco.

label: Second Empire Style
defn: The Napoleon III-era style of mansard roofs and rich Baroque-Renaissance ornament, spread from Paris to the Americas: the Palais Garnier, Philadelphia City Hall, the Eisenhower Executive Office Building.
aliases: Napoleon III style; Second Empire architecture

label: Baroque Revival Architecture
defn: The late 19th- and early 20th-century revival of Baroque massing and ornament for public buildings and theatres: the Berlin Cathedral, Edwardian Baroque town halls.

label: Greek Revival Architecture
defn: The late 18th- and 19th-century revival of Greek temple forms and orders, dominant in the United States and northern Europe: the Second Bank of the United States, the Altes Museum, St George's Hall, Liverpool.

label: Egyptian Revival Architecture
defn: The revival of ancient Egyptian pylons, obelisks and lotus columns after Napoleon's Egyptian campaign, in cemeteries, prisons, synagogues and cinemas: the Egyptian Hall, Piccadilly, the Tombs, New York.

label: Beaux-Arts Architecture
defn: The academic classical architecture taught at the École des Beaux-Arts in Paris (c. 1830–1920), symmetrical and richly sculpted, carried to the Americas: the Petit Palais, New York Public Library, Grand Central Terminal.

label: Eclecticism in Architecture
defn: Nineteenth- and early 20th-century architecture freely combining historical styles in one building: Gründerzeit apartment blocks, Stile Umbertino palaces of Rome, Russian eclectic mansions.

label: Victorian Architecture
defn: The succession of revival and picturesque styles built in Britain and its empire and in North America during Victoria's reign (1837–1901): Stick style houses, Eastlake villas, Australian Victorian terraces.

label: Queen Anne Style Architecture
defn: The late 19th-century British and American domestic style of red brick or shingle, asymmetrical towers, bays and turrets: Norman Shaw's Swan House, the Carson Mansion.

label: Shingle Style Architecture
defn: The American seaside and suburban house style of the 1880s wrapped in continuous wood shingles: the Isaac Bell House, the William Watts Sherman House.

label: Colonial Revival Architecture
defn: The American (and Brazilian) revival from the 1876 Centennial of colonial Georgian and Dutch forms: Georgian Revival houses, Dutch Colonial Revival gambrel houses.

label: Spanish Colonial Revival Architecture
defn: The early 20th-century revival of Spanish colonial forms in California, Florida and the American Southwest, after the 1915 Panama–California Exposition: Santa Barbara County Courthouse, the California Building, San Diego.

label: Mission Revival Architecture
defn: The Californian revival (1890–1920) of the Spanish missions' arcades, curved parapets and bell towers: the Mission Inn, Riverside, the Santa Fe Depot, San Diego.

label: Pueblo Revival Architecture
defn: The 20th-century revival in New Mexico and Arizona of Pueblo and Spanish adobe forms: the New Mexico Museum of Art, La Fonda on the Plaza.

label: Mayan Revival Architecture
defn: The 1920s–1930s American revival of Maya and Mesoamerican ornament: Frank Lloyd Wright's Hollyhock House, the Mayan Theater, Los Angeles.

label: Neo-Manueline
defn: The Portuguese and Brazilian revival (from the 1840s) of Manueline ornament: Pena Palace, Rossio Station, the Royal Portuguese Cabinet of Reading, Rio.

label: Russian Revival Architecture
defn: The 19th-century revival of medieval Muscovite and Byzantine-Russian forms in the Russian Empire: the State Historical Museum, the Church of the Savior on Blood, the Upper Trading Rows.

label: Russian Neoclassical Revival
defn: The revival of Russian Neoclassicism and Empire style in the Russian Empire c. 1900–1917 (retrospectivism): Fomin's Polovtsov Dacha, Zholtovsky's Tarasov House.

label: Romanian Revival Architecture
defn: The Romanian national style (from the 1880s) reviving Brâncovenesc and Moldavian forms: Ion Mincu's Lahovari House, Mincu's Bufetul de la Șosea.

label: National Romantic Style
defn: The Nordic and Baltic national architecture of c. 1890–1920 drawing on vernacular and medieval forms: Helsinki Central Station, Stockholm City Hall, Norwegian dragestil.

label: Zakopane Style
defn: The Polish national style created by Stanisław Witkiewicz (1890s) from Podhale highland timber building: Villa Koliba, the Chapel in Jaszczurówka.

label: Swiss Chalet Style
defn: The 19th-century picturesque revival of the Alpine timber chalet, built across Europe and Scandinavia: Norwegian sveitserstil villas, spa pavilions.

label: Federation Architecture
defn: The Australian architecture of c. 1890–1915, combining Queen Anne, Arts and Crafts and Romanesque elements: Federation Queen Anne houses, the Queen Victoria Building.

label: Rustic Architecture
defn: The North American log-and-stone style of the Adirondack Great Camps and the national parks (1870s–1940s): Old Faithful Inn, Timberline Lodge.

label: Ancient Egyptian Architecture
defn: The stone architecture of pharaonic Egypt (c. 3000 BC – AD 300): pyramids, temples and rock-cut tombs: the Pyramids of Giza, Karnak, Abu Simbel.

label: Architecture of Mesopotamia
defn: The mud-brick architecture of Sumer, Babylonia and Assyria: ziggurats, temples, palaces and city walls: the Ziggurat of Ur, the Ishtar Gate, the palaces of Nimrud.
aliases: Mesopotamian architecture; Assyrian architecture; Babylonian architecture

label: Achaemenid Architecture
defn: The palace and tomb architecture of the Persian empire (550–330 BC): Persepolis, Pasargadae, Naqsh-e Rostam.

label: Parthian Architecture
defn: The architecture of the Arsacid empire (247 BC – AD 224), with the first monumental iwans and Hellenistic ornament: Hatra, Nisa, Ashur's Parthian palace.

label: Sasanian Architecture
defn: The architecture of the Sasanian empire (224–651): vaulted iwans, squinch domes and fire temples: Taq Kasra, Palace of Ardashir, Takht-e Soleyman.

label: Minoan Architecture
defn: The Bronze Age palace architecture of Crete (c. 2000–1450 BC): Knossos, Phaistos, Malia.

label: Mycenaean Architecture
defn: The Late Bronze Age citadels, megara and tholos tombs of mainland Greece: the Lion Gate, Mycenae, the Treasury of Atreus, Tiryns.

label: Ancient Greek Architecture
defn: The architecture of the Greek world from the Archaic to the Hellenistic period, defined by the temple and the orders: the Parthenon, the Temple of Hephaestus, the Theatre of Epidaurus.

label: Etruscan Architecture
defn: The architecture of the Etruscans (c. 900–27 BC): timber-and-terracotta temples, arched gates and rock-cut tombs: the Banditaccia necropolis, the Arch of Augustus, Perugia.

label: Ancient Roman Architecture
defn: The architecture of Rome and its empire (c. 500 BC – AD 400), of the arch, vault, dome and concrete: the Pantheon, the Colosseum, the Pont du Gard.

label: Nabataean Architecture
defn: The rock-cut tomb and temple façades of the Nabataeans (1st century BC – 2nd century AD): Al-Khazneh, Ad Deir at Petra, Hegra.

label: Early Christian Architecture
defn: The church architecture of the late Roman empire (4th–6th century): basilicas, baptisteries and martyria: Old St Peter's, Santa Sabina, the Mausoleum of Galla Placidia.
aliases: Early Christian art and architecture; Paleochristian architecture

label: Byzantine Architecture
defn: The architecture of the Eastern Roman empire (c. 330–1453): domed churches on pendentives and the cross-in-square plan: Hagia Sophia, San Vitale, Ravenna, Hosios Loukas.

label: Serbo-Byzantine Architecture
defn: The medieval church architecture of Serbia (12th–15th century) in its Raška, Vardar and Morava schools: Studenica, Gračanica, Ravanica.

label: Architecture of Kievan Rus'
defn: The church architecture of Kievan Rus' and its successor principalities (10th–13th century): Saint Sophia Cathedral, Kyiv, Saint Sophia, Novgorod, the Church of the Intercession on the Nerl.

label: Armenian Architecture
defn: The stone church architecture of Armenia from the 4th century, with domed central plans and carved khachkars: Etchmiadzin Cathedral, Zvartnots, the Cathedral of the Holy Cross, Aghtamar.
aliases: Architecture of Armenia; Armenian church architecture

label: Architecture of Georgia
defn: The medieval church and fortress architecture of Georgia (Caucasus): Jvari, Svetitskhoveli, Bagrati Cathedral.

label: Pre-Romanesque Architecture
defn: The architecture of western Europe between the end of Rome and c. 1000: Visigothic, Asturian, Anglo-Saxon, Lombard and Mozarabic churches: Santa María del Naranco, San Juan de Baños, Escomb Church.

label: Carolingian Architecture
defn: The architecture of the Carolingian empire (c. 780–900), reviving Roman forms: the Palatine Chapel, Aachen, the Lorsch gatehouse, Germigny-des-Prés.

label: Ottonian Architecture
defn: The architecture of the Ottonian empire (c. 936–1056) leading into Romanesque: St. Michael's Church, Hildesheim, St. Cyriakus, Gernrode.

label: Romanesque Architecture
defn: The round-arched, massive-walled architecture of Europe c. 1000–1200, with its regional schools: Speyer Cathedral, Sainte-Foy, Conques, Durham Cathedral, Pisa Cathedral.

label: Arab-Norman Architecture
defn: The architecture of Norman Sicily (1091–1194) combining Latin, Byzantine and Islamic forms: the Palatine Chapel, Palermo, Monreale Cathedral, the Zisa.

label: Moldavian Style
defn: The church architecture of medieval Moldavia (15th–16th century), Gothic-Byzantine in plan with painted exteriors: Voroneț, Sucevița, Putna Monastery.

label: Gothic Architecture
defn: Medieval European architecture of the pointed arch, rib vault and flying buttress (c. 1140–1520): Chartres Cathedral, Sainte-Chapelle, Cologne Cathedral.

label: Tudor Architecture
defn: The English architecture of 1485–1603, late Perpendicular Gothic turning to Renaissance: Hampton Court Palace, King's College Chapel, Hardwick Hall.

label: Plateresque
defn: The Spanish style of c. 1490–1560 covering façades in fine silversmith-like Renaissance ornament: the University of Salamanca façade, San Esteban, Salamanca, Acolman.

label: Manueline
defn: The Portuguese late Gothic style of the reign of Manuel I (1495–1521), with maritime and twisted-rope ornament: Jerónimos Monastery, Belém Tower, the Convent of Christ, Tomar.

label: Herrerian Style
defn: The austere classical style of Juan de Herrera for Philip II (from 1567): El Escorial, Valladolid Cathedral, the Archivo de Indias.

label: Churrigueresque
defn: The late Baroque style of Spain and New Spain (c. 1700–1760) with estípite pilasters and dense ornament: the Sagrario Metropolitano, Mexico City, the Transparente, Toledo.

label: Rococo Architecture
defn: The late Baroque architecture and interior style of c. 1730–1770, light, asymmetrical and ornamental: Sanssouci, the Wieskirche, the Amalienburg.

label: Uzorochye
defn: The ornate Muscovite church and palace architecture of the 17th century, with tented roofs, kokoshniki and tilework: the Church of the Nativity in Putinki, the churches of Yaroslavl.

label: Brâncovenesc Style
defn: The Wallachian style of Constantin Brâncoveanu's reign (1688–1714) combining Renaissance, Baroque and Ottoman elements: Horezu Monastery, Mogoșoaia Palace.

label: Palladian Architecture
defn: The architecture derived from Andrea Palladio's villas and treatise, revived in 18th-century Britain, Ireland and America: Villa Rotonda, Chiswick House, Monticello.

label: Georgian Architecture
defn: The British and colonial American classical architecture of 1714–1830, in brick and stone terraces, houses and churches: the Royal Crescent, Bath, Merrion Square, colonial Williamsburg.

label: Empire Style
defn: The Napoleonic phase of Neoclassicism (c. 1800–1830), spread across Europe and Russia: the Arc de Triomphe du Carrousel, La Madeleine, the Russian Empire buildings of St Petersburg.

label: Federal Architecture
defn: The American classical architecture of c. 1780–1830, after Adam and Palladio: the White House, Massachusetts State House, the Gardner–Pingree House.

label: Pombaline Style
defn: The rational, earthquake-resistant style of the rebuilding of Lisbon after 1755: the Baixa Pombalina, Praça do Comércio.

label: Architecture of the Bulgarian Revival
defn: The Bulgarian urban houses, churches and schools of the National Revival (18th–19th century): Plovdiv Old Town, Koprivshtitsa, the Rila Monastery's residential wings.

label: American Colonial Architecture
defn: The architecture of the English colonies of North America (17th–18th century): First Period timber houses, saltbox and Cape Cod types, Georgian brick: the Paul Revere House, Westover Plantation.

label: Spanish Colonial Architecture
defn: The architecture of the Spanish empire in the Americas and the Philippines (16th–19th century): missions, cathedrals and plazas: the Mission San Xavier del Bac, Cusco Cathedral, the Baroque churches of the Philippines.

label: Andean Baroque
defn: The mestizo Baroque of the colonial Andes (c. 1680–1780) with flat carved Indigenous-inflected ornament: San Lorenzo, Potosí, the Jesuit Church of Arequipa.

label: Portuguese Colonial Architecture
defn: The architecture of the Portuguese empire in Brazil, Africa and Asia (16th–19th century): the historic centre of Ouro Preto, Salvador's Pelourinho, the churches of Old Goa.

label: French Colonial Architecture
defn: The architecture of the French colonies in North America and the Caribbean: raised galleried Creole houses and Quebec stone houses: the Bolduc House, the French Quarter, New Orleans.

label: Dutch Colonial Architecture
defn: The architecture of the Dutch colonies (New Netherland, the East Indies, Suriname), with gambrel and stepped-gable roofs: the Jan Martense Schenck House, Dutch colonial houses of Batavia.

label: Cape Dutch Architecture
defn: The whitewashed, thatched, ornate-gabled farmhouses of the Dutch Cape Colony (17th–18th century): Groot Constantia, Vergelegen.

label: Renaissance Architecture
defn: European architecture c. 1400–1600 reviving classical orders: Brunelleschi's Duomo dome, Bramante's Tempietto, Palladio's Villa Rotonda.

label: Baroque Architecture
defn: European and colonial architecture c. 1600–1750 of movement and spatial drama: Borromini's San Carlo, Versailles, Melk Abbey.

label: Neoclassical Architecture
defn: Architecture c. 1750–1850 on Greek and Roman models: the Panthéon, Paris, the British Museum, the Brandenburg Gate.

label: Arts and Crafts Architecture
defn: The domestic architecture of the Arts and Crafts movement (c. 1860–1920), vernacular materials and honest craftsmanship: the Red House, Voysey's Broadleys, the Gamble House.
aliases: Arts and Crafts movement; Domestic Revival

label: Chicago School
defn: The steel-frame commercial architecture of Chicago (1880s–1910s), the first skyscrapers: the Home Insurance Building, the Monadnock Building, the Carson Pirie Scott Building.

label: Prairie School
defn: The Midwestern American architecture of Frank Lloyd Wright and his circle (c. 1900–1917), low and horizontal: Robie House, Unity Temple, the Darwin D. Martin House.

label: Czech Cubism
defn: The Cubist architecture of Bohemia (1910–1925), with faceted crystalline façades and its later rondocubist phase: the House of the Black Madonna, the Kovařovic Villa, the Adria Palace.

label: Expressionist Architecture
defn: The early 20th-century European architecture of distorted, sculptural and crystalline form, in brick and concrete: the Einstein Tower, the Chilehaus, Het Schip.

label: Futurist Architecture
defn: The architecture of speed and the machine announced by Sant'Elia (1914) and its later heirs, from Googie to neo-futurism: Sant'Elia's Città Nuova, the Theme Building, LAX.

label: Art Deco Architecture
defn: The architecture of Art Deco (c. 1920–1940), geometric, stepped and ornamented, with its Streamline Moderne phase: the Chrysler Building, Miami Beach's Art Deco District, Napier.

label: Bauhaus Architecture
defn: The architecture of the Bauhaus school and its masters (1919–1933) and its diaspora: the Bauhaus Dessau, the Masters' Houses, Tel Aviv's White City.

label: International Style
defn: The modern architecture named by Hitchcock and Johnson (1932): volume rather than mass, regularity, no applied ornament: Villa Savoye, the Barcelona Pavilion, the Seagram Building.

label: Constructivist Architecture
defn: The Soviet avant-garde architecture of the 1920s–early 1930s: the Shukhov Tower, the Narkomfin Building, the Rusakov Workers' Club.

label: Reform Architecture
defn: The German-speaking reform movement of c. 1900–1930 that rejected historicism for simple, regional building (Heimatschutz, Um 1800): Paul Schultze-Naumburg's Cecilienhof, Hellerau.

label: Traditionalist School
defn: The Dutch traditionalist architecture of c. 1900–1960 in brick and tile, with its Delft and Bossche schools: Granpré Molière's Vreewijk, Dom Hans van der Laan's Roosenberg Abbey.

label: Nordic Classicism
defn: The pared-down classical architecture of Scandinavia and Finland c. 1910–1930: Asplund's Stockholm City Library, the Woodland Chapel, Aalto's early Jyväskylä buildings.

label: Stripped Classicism
defn: The simplified, unornamented classicism of the 1920s–1940s for government buildings in democracies and dictatorships alike: the Federal Reserve Board Building, the Palais de Chaillot.

label: Stalinist Architecture
defn: The monumental socialist-realist architecture of the USSR and its satellites (1933–1955): the Seven Sisters, the Palace of Culture and Science, Karl-Marx-Allee.

label: Fascist Architecture
defn: The architecture of Fascist Italy (1922–1943), from rationalism to monumental stripped classicism: EUR, Rome, the Casa del Fascio, Como, the Palazzo della Civiltà Italiana.
aliases: Stile Littorio; architecture of the Fascist period

label: Nazi Architecture
defn: The architecture of the Third Reich (1933–1945), monumental neoclassical for the state and Heimatstil for housing: the Nuremberg Rally Grounds, Tempelhof Airport, the Reich Chancellery.

label: Mid-Century Modern Architecture
defn: The American-led domestic and commercial modernism of c. 1945–1970: post-and-beam houses, glass pavilions and regional variants: the Eames House, the Stahl House, Miami Modern hotels.

label: High-tech Architecture
defn: Late-modern architecture from the 1970s that expresses structure and services as industrial technology: the Centre Pompidou, the Lloyd's Building, HSBC Main Building, Hong Kong.

label: New Classical Architecture
defn: Contemporary classical and traditional architecture since the 1980s: Poundbury, Robert Adam's Sackler Library, the Schermerhorn Symphony Center.

label: Art Nouveau Architecture
defn: Architecture of the Art Nouveau c. 1890–1914: Horta's Hôtel Tassel, Guimard's Métro entrances, Gaudí's Casa Batlló.

label: Modern Architecture
defn: Architecture of the modern movement (c. 1900–1975): functionalism, the International Style and their regional forms: Villa Savoye, the Barcelona Pavilion, Fallingwater.

label: Brutalist Architecture
defn: Modernist architecture of the 1950s–1970s in exposed concrete and massive forms: Unité d'Habitation, the Barbican Estate, Boston City Hall.

label: Postmodern Architecture
defn: Architecture from the 1960s–1990s returning to ornament, history and irony: Venturi's Vanna Venturi House, Graves's Portland Building, Stirling's Neue Staatsgalerie.

label: Deconstructivism
defn: Architecture from the 1980s of fragmented, non-rectilinear forms: Gehry's Guggenheim Bilbao, Libeskind's Jewish Museum Berlin, Hadid's Vitra Fire Station.

label: Contemporary Architecture
defn: Architecture by architects born from 1945, in plural idioms from parametric design to vernacular-sustainable building: Kéré's Gando school, SANAA's Rolex Learning Center.

label: Nagara Architecture
defn: The northern Hindu and Jain temple tradition whose sanctum rises in a curvilinear shikhara of stacked courses (latina, shekhari and bhumija forms): Kandariya Mahadeva at Khajuraho, Mahabodhi Temple, Kopeshwar temple, Khidrapur.
aliases: Nagara style;North Indian temple architecture;Indo-Aryan temple style

label: Kalinga Architecture
defn: The Odishan temple tradition of the rekha, pidha and khakhara deula with jagamohana halls (7th–13th century): Lingaraja Temple, Konark Sun Temple, Jagannath Temple, Puri.

label: Maru-Gurjara Architecture
defn: The temple tradition of Gujarat and Rajasthan (11th–13th century and its revival) with richly carved marble interiors, especially for Jain patrons: Dilwara temples, Mount Abu, Modhera Sun Temple, Ranakpur.

label: Dravidian Architecture
defn: The southern Hindu temple tradition of stepped pyramidal vimanas, pillared mandapas and monumental gopurams in walled precincts: Shore Temple, Mahabalipuram, Brihadisvara Temple, Thanjavur, Meenakshi Temple, Madurai, Virupaksha Temple, Hampi.
aliases: Dravida style;South Indian temple architecture;Tamil architecture;kovil

label: Vesara
defn: The Deccan temple tradition combining Nagara and Dravidian forms, developed under the Chalukyas and Hoysalas: Pattadakal, Mahadeva Temple, Itagi, Chennakesava Temple, Belur, Hoysaleswara Temple, Halebidu.

label: Kerala Architecture
defn: The timber-and-laterite building tradition of Kerala with steep tiled and copper roofs: circular and rectangular sreekovil temples, koothambalam theatres, nalukettu houses and palaces: Vadakkunnathan Temple, Padmanabhapuram Palace, Mattancherry Palace.

label: Bengal Temple Architecture
defn: The brick and terracotta temples of Bengal (16th–19th century) whose curved roofs translate the thatched hut: the chala types (do-chala, char-chala, at-chala), jor-bangla and the ratna (pinnacled) types: Jor Bangla Temple, Bishnupur, Rasmancha, Dakshineswar Kali Temple.
aliases: Bengal temple style;terracotta temples of Bengal

label: Buddhist Architecture
defn: The architecture of Buddhism in its South Asian homeland: stupas, chaitya halls and vihara monasteries from the Mauryas to the Palas, and the monasteries of Gandhara: Great Stupa, Sanchi, Dhamek Stupa, Nalanda Mahavihara, Takht-i-Bahi.

label: Indian Rock-cut Architecture
defn: Caves, halls and monolithic temples excavated from living rock (3rd century BCE–10th century): Ajanta Caves, Karla chaitya, Kailasa Temple, Ellora, Elephanta Caves.

label: Sinhalese Architecture
defn: The Buddhist and royal architecture of Sri Lanka: dagobas, vatadages, image houses and monasteries of Anuradhapura and Polonnaruwa, and the timber halls of the Kandyan kingdom: Ruwanweli Maha Seya, Jetavanaramaya, Gal Vihara, Temple of the Tooth.
aliases: architecture of Sri Lanka;Sri Lankan Buddhist architecture

label: Newar Architecture
defn: The brick-and-timber architecture of the Newars of the Kathmandu valley: multi-roofed pagoda temples, shikhara temples, stupas, bahal courtyards and palace squares with carved struts and windows: Pashupatinath, Nyatapola, Changu Narayan, Swayambhunath.

label: Tibetan Buddhist Architecture
defn: The monastic and palace architecture of Tibet and the Tibetan Buddhist world: battered stone-and-earth walls, flat roofs, gilded roofs, chortens and kumbums: Potala Palace, Jokhang, Drepung, Gyantse Kumbum.

label: Dzong Architecture
defn: The fortress-monasteries of Bhutan and Tibet housing civil and monastic administration around a central utse tower: Punakha Dzong, Paro Rinpung Dzong, Trongsa Dzong.

label: Rajput Architecture
defn: The forts, palaces, havelis and cenotaphs of the Rajput kingdoms of Rajasthan and Central India (8th–19th century), with jharokhas and chhatris: Amber Fort, Chittorgarh Fort, Kumbhalgarh, Jaisalmer Fort.

label: Stepwell
defn: The stepped subterranean wells of western India built as civic and devotional monuments, Hindu and Islamic (vav, baoli): Rani ki vav, Adalaj Stepwell, Chand Baori.

label: Sikh Architecture
defn: The gurdwaras and memorials of the Sikh tradition (17th–19th century) drawing on Mughal and Rajput forms, with fluted domes and gilded upper storeys: Harmandir Sahib, Takht Sri Patna Sahib, Gurdwara Baba Atal.

label: Harappan Architecture
defn: The planned fired-brick cities of the Indus Valley Civilisation (c. 2600–1900 BCE): grid streets, drains, granaries and citadels: Great Bath, Mohenjo-daro, Harappa, Dholavira.

label: Haveli
defn: the courtyard townhouse and mansion of north India and Pakistan, inward-looking round one or more chowks, with carved jharokhas and often painted walls: the havelis of Shekhawati, Jaisalmer's Patwon ki Haveli, Old Delhi and Lahore havelis.

label: Kashmiri Houseboat
defn: the moored cedar houseboat of Srinagar's Dal and Nageen lakes (from the early 1900s), built and run by the Hanji, with carved walnut panelling and khatamband ceilings.

label: Assam-type House
defn: the light timber- or bamboo-framed house of Assam and north-east India (late 19th–20th century), on a raised plinth with steep roof and wide veranda, built for monsoon and earthquake: bungalows of Shillong and Guwahati.

label: Chinese Architecture
defn: The classical timber-frame tradition of China, with bracket sets (dougong), raised platforms and sweeping tiled roofs, used for palaces, altars, temples, pagodas and gateways and codified in official manuals (Yingzao Fashi): Forbidden City, Temple of Heaven, Foguang Temple, Giant Wild Goose Pagoda.

label: Siheyuan
defn: The north-Chinese courtyard house of four halls round a central yard, the model of the Beijing hutong: Prince Gong Mansion, Qiao Family Compound.

label: Yaodong
defn: The earth-sheltered cave dwellings of the Loess Plateau, cut into cliffs, sunk round pit courtyards or built as vaults.

label: Hakka Walled Village
defn: The fortified communal dwellings of the Hakka and Minnan of southern China: the earthen tulou of Fujian, weilongwu and walled villages: Tianluokeng tulou cluster, Chengqi Lou.

label: Hui-style Architecture
defn: The merchant houses, ancestral halls and memorial arches of Huizhou (southern Anhui), with whitewashed walls, stepped horse-head gables and carved brick, wood and stone: Xidi, Hongcun.

label: Lingnan Architecture
defn: The building tradition of Guangdong and Guangxi: wok-ear gables, ceramic ridge figures, arcaded qilou shophouses and Lingnan gardens: Chen Clan Ancestral Hall, Foshan Ancestral Temple.

label: Hokkien Architecture
defn: The Minnan building tradition of southern Fujian, Taiwan and the Hokkien diaspora: swallowtail ridges, red brick and cut-porcelain (jian nian) roof decoration on temples and houses: Bangka Lungshan Temple, Kaiyuan Temple, Quanzhou.

label: Sichuanese Architecture
defn: The timber and stilted vernacular of Sichuan and Chongqing (chuan-dou framing, diaojiaolou), with its Song–Yuan temple halls.

label: Shikumen
defn: The Shanghai lane-house (lilong) type of the 1860s–1930s joining a Chinese courtyard plan to Western terrace housing behind stone-framed gates: Xintiandi, Tianzifang.

label: Shinto Shrine Architecture
defn: The architecture of Japanese Shinto shrines (jinja) in named styles (zukuri) defined by roof, entrance and plan: Ise Grand Shrine (shinmei), Izumo Taisha (taisha), Kamigamo Shrine (nagare), Nikkō Tōshō-gū (gongen).

label: Japanese Buddhist Architecture
defn: The temple architecture of Japanese Buddhism in its named styles: wayō, daibutsuyō, zenshūyō and the mixed setchūyō, with pagodas, halls, gates and storehouses: Hōryū-ji, Tōdai-ji, Byōdō-in, Engaku-ji Shariden.

label: Shinden-zukuri
defn: The Heian aristocratic residence of a main hall facing a south garden and pond, linked to wings by corridors: Kyoto Imperial Palace Shishinden, Byōdō-in (derived).

label: Shoin-zukuri
defn: The warrior-class residential style of the Muromachi to Edo periods with tatami rooms, tokonoma alcove, staggered shelves, built-in desk and sliding fusuma: Ninomaru Palace, Nijō Castle, Kojō-in, Onjō-ji.

label: Sukiya-zukuri
defn: The informal residential and tea-house style derived from the chashitsu, using natural materials and restrained finish: Katsura Imperial Villa, Tai-an, Jo-an.

label: Minka
defn: The vernacular houses of Japan's farmers, craftsmen and merchants: farmhouses (nōka) and townhouses (machiya), in regional types such as gasshō-zukuri and magariya: Shirakawa-gō, Kyoto machiya.

label: Japanese Castle Architecture
defn: The fortified residences of the daimyō (16th–17th century): stone ramparts, moats, gates and the multi-storey tenshu keep: Himeji Castle, Matsumoto Castle, Osaka Castle.

label: Kofun
defn: The mounded tombs of Japan's Kofun period (3rd–7th century), above all the keyhole-shaped zenpō-kōen-fun, often moated and set with haniwa: Daisen Kofun, Mozu-Furuichi kofun group, Ishibutai Kofun.

label: Ryukyuan Architecture
defn: The architecture of the Ryukyu kingdom (Okinawa): red-tiled gusuku castles and palaces, utaki sacred groves and turtleback and gable-roofed tombs: Shuri Castle, Tamaudun, Nakagusuku Castle.

label: Giyōfū Architecture
defn: The pseudo-Western buildings of early Meiji Japan (1860s–1880s) made by Japanese carpenters imitating Western forms in timber and plaster: Former Kaichi School, Tsukiji Hotel, Former Saiseikan Hospital.

label: Korean Architecture
defn: The timber-frame architecture of Korea's palaces, temples, shrines and fortresses, classified by bracket system (jusimpo, dapo, ikgong) and painted in dancheong: Gyeongbokgung, Bulguksa, Jongmyo, Haeinsa Janggyeong Panjeon.

label: Hanok
defn: The traditional Korean house with ondol-heated rooms, wooden maru floors and tiled or thatched roofs, set by geomancy: Bukchon Hanok Village, Hahoe Folk Village, Yangdong Village.

label: Khmer Architecture
defn: The temple-mountains, galleried enclosures and prasat towers of the Khmer empire and its predecessors (7th–13th century) in successive named styles (Sambor Prei Kuk, Preah Ko, Bakheng, Banteay Srei, Baphuon, Angkor Wat, Bayon): Angkor Wat, Banteay Srei, Bayon, Preah Vihear.

label: Candi Architecture
defn: The Hindu and Buddhist stone temples and stupas of classical Indonesia (7th–15th century), in the Central Javanese (Mataram) and East Javanese (Singhasari, Majapahit) styles and in Sumatra: Borobudur, Prambanan, Candi Penataran, Muara Takus.

label: Balinese Architecture
defn: The Hindu-Balinese building tradition of walled pura temples with split gates (candi bentar), meru towers and pavilions, and compound houses laid out by cosmological axes: Pura Besakih, Pura Taman Ayun, Pura Ulun Danu Bratan.

label: Javanese Traditional House
defn: The timber houses of Java in ranked roof types (joglo, limasan, kampung) with the open pendopo pavilion in front: Kraton Yogyakarta pendopo, Mangkunegaran Palace.

label: Burmese Architecture
defn: The Buddhist architecture of Myanmar: bell-shaped zedi stupas, hollow gu temples, pyatthat spires and teak monasteries, from Pagan to Mandalay: Ananda Temple, Shwezigon, Shwedagon Pagoda, Shwenandaw Monastery.

label: Thai Architecture
defn: The Buddhist and royal architecture of Thailand, in the art-historical styles of Sukhothai, Lanna, Ayutthaya and Rattanakosin: wat compounds with ubosot, vihara, chedi, prang and mondop: Wat Mahathat, Sukhothai, Wat Phra Si Sanphet, Wat Phrathat Doi Suthep, Wat Phra Kaew.

label: Lao Architecture
defn: The Buddhist architecture of Laos (Lan Xang) in the Luang Prabang, Vientiane and Xieng Khouang temple styles with sweeping multi-tiered roofs and that stupas: Wat Xieng Thong, Pha That Luang, Wat Si Saket.

label: Cham Architecture
defn: The brick tower-temples (kalan) of the Champa kingdoms in central and southern Vietnam (7th–15th century) in successive styles (Mỹ Sơn E1, Đồng Dương, Tháp Mắm): Mỹ Sơn, Po Nagar, Po Klong Garai.

label: Vietnamese Architecture
defn: The timber architecture of Vietnam's pagodas (chùa), communal houses (đình), citadels and imperial tombs, from the Lý to the Nguyễn: One Pillar Pagoda, Temple of Literature, Thiên Mụ Pagoda, Imperial City of Huế.

label: Batak Architecture
defn: The saddle-roofed timber houses (rumah adat) and granaries of the Batak peoples of North Sumatra, raised on piles and carved and painted with gorga ornament.

label: Bahay Kubo
defn: The Philippine nipa hut: a stilted house of bamboo and timber with a thatched nipa roof, the base type of lowland Filipino vernacular.

label: Bahay na Bato
defn: The Spanish-colonial Filipino town house (18th–19th century) with a stone lower storey and a timber upper storey with capiz-shell sliding windows: Vigan, Casa Manila.

label: Sino-Portuguese Architecture
defn: The shophouses and mansions of Phuket, Penang and the Straits Settlements (late 19th–early 20th century) mixing Hokkien plans with European façades.

label: Malay Traditional House
defn: the stilted timber house of the Malay world, joined without nails, with steep thatched or tiled roofs and carved panels, in regional types: rumah limas, rumah bumbung panjang, Minangkabau rumah gadang.
aliases: rumah Melayu; rumah tradisional Melayu; Malay house

label: Aksumite Architecture
defn: The stone architecture of the Aksumite kingdom (1st–7th century) with its 'monkey-head' timber-and-rubble walls, palaces and carved monolithic stelae: Northern Stelae Field, Aksum, Dungur palace, Debre Damo.

label: Ethiopian Rock-hewn Churches
defn: The monolithic and semi-monolithic churches carved from rock in Ethiopia (10th–13th century and later): Bete Giyorgis, Lalibela, Bete Medhane Alem, Abuna Yemata Guh.
aliases: rock-hewn churches of Lalibela;Tigray rock churches

label: Gondarine Architecture
defn: The castle-palaces and churches of the Gondar period (17th–18th century), with battlemented towers and domes: Fasil Ghebbi, Fasilides' Bath, Debre Berhan Selassie.

label: Nubian Pyramids
defn: The steep pyramids, temples and palaces of the Kushite kingdoms of Napata and Meroë (8th century BCE–4th century CE): Meroë, Jebel Barkal, El-Kurru, Musawwarat es-Sufra.

label: Great Zimbabwe
defn: The dry-stone architecture of the Zimbabwe culture (11th–19th century): mortarless granite enclosures, coursed walls with chevron and chequer friezes: Great Zimbabwe, Khami, Mapungubwe, Naletale.

label: Ksar
defn: The fortified earthen and stone villages, granaries (agadir, ghorfa) and kasbahs of the Amazigh and Saharan world: Aït Benhaddou, Ksar of Ouadane, Ksar Ouled Soltane, Ghardaïa (M'zab).

label: Hausa Architecture
defn: The earthen architecture of the Hausa city-states of northern Nigeria and Niger: domed and vaulted mud houses and palaces with relief façades (zanko pinnacles): Gidan Rumfa, Kano, Zaria Friday Mosque.

label: Maya Architecture
defn: The stone architecture of the Maya (c. 1000 BCE–1500 CE): stepped pyramid-temples, palaces with corbel vaults, ballcourts and stelae plazas, in the regional styles Petén, Usumacinta, Río Bec, Chenes and Puuc: Tikal Temple I, Temple of the Inscriptions, Palenque, Uxmal, Chichen Itza.

label: Mesoamerican Architecture
defn: The monumental architecture of non-Maya Mesoamerica: Olmec mounds, the talud-tablero platforms of Teotihuacan, Zapotec and Mixtec Oaxaca, Classic Veracruz and Toltec Tula: Pyramid of the Sun, Monte Albán, Mitla, Pyramid of the Niches, El Tajín.

label: Aztec Architecture
defn: The architecture of the Mexica and their Late Postclassic neighbours (14th–16th century): twin-temple pyramids, palaces and causeway cities: Templo Mayor, Tenayuca, Santa Cecilia Acatitlan, Malinalco.

label: Inca Architecture
defn: The fitted-masonry architecture of Tawantinsuyu (15th–16th century): ashlar and polygonal walls, trapezoidal doorways and niches, terraces, roads and tambos: Machu Picchu, Sacsayhuamán, Coricancha, Ollantaytambo.

label: Andean Architecture
defn: The monumental architecture of the Andes before the Inca: Caral's platform mounds, Chavín's galleried temple, Moche adobe huacas, Tiwanaku's stone platforms, Wari administrative centres, Chimú Chan Chan and Chachapoya Kuélap.

label: Ancestral Puebloan Architecture
defn: The masonry and adobe great houses, cliff dwellings, kivas and terraced pueblos of the Ancestral Puebloans and their descendants in the US Southwest: Pueblo Bonito, Chaco Canyon, Cliff Palace, Mesa Verde, Taos Pueblo.

label: Mound Builders
defn: The earthen platform mounds, effigy mounds and geometric earthworks of the Eastern Woodlands (Archaic to Mississippian, c. 3500 BCE–1600 CE): Poverty Point, Hopewell Ceremonial Earthworks, Monks Mound, Cahokia, Serpent Mound.

label: Wharenui
defn: The carved Māori meeting house on the marae, its frame read as the body of an ancestor: Te Hau ki Tūranga, Te Tokanganui-a-Noho, Rauru.

label: Fale
defn: The Samoan open-sided house with a domed thatched roof on posts, including the round fale tele guest house.

label: Maneaba
defn: The great community meeting house of Kiribati and Tuvalu, a vast thatched roof on low posts.

label: Haus Tambaran
defn: The spirit and men's houses of the Sepik region of Papua New Guinea with soaring painted gable façades.

label: Marae
defn: The stone-paved ceremonial platforms and courts of East Polynesia, including the image ahu of Rapa Nui with their moai: Taputapuātea, Ahu Tongariki, Ahu Tahai.

label: Nan Madol
defn: The basalt-prism megalithic architecture of the Saudeleur polity on Pohnpei (c. 1180–1628) and Leluh on Kosrae: artificial islets of stacked columnar basalt.

label: Chilotan Architecture
defn: The shingled timber architecture of the Chiloé archipelago, above all the Jesuit-founded wooden churches built by local boatwrights (18th–19th century): Church of Castro, Church of Achao, palafitos of Castro.
aliases: Chiloé School of religious wooden architecture

label: British Vernacular Architecture
defn: the traditional houses and farm buildings of Britain and Ireland in local materials, studied by regional type and by framing and walling tradition: Wealden hall houses, cruck-framed halls, Devon cob, Hebridean blackhouses, Dartmoor longhouses, border bastles.
aliases: vernacular architecture of Britain; English vernacular architecture; British vernacular building

label: German Vernacular Architecture
defn: the traditional timber-framed (Fachwerk) and log-and-frame houses and farmhouses of the German-speaking lands, studied by regional house type: the Low German hall house, the Black Forest house, the Umgebinde house of Upper Lusatia, half-timbered towns such as Quedlinburg.

label: Kulla
defn: the fortified stone tower house of Albania and Kosovo (17th–19th century), with a stone ground floor and a timber-galleried upper oda: Kulla of Mazrek (Junik), the kullas of Dukagjin and Gjirokastër.

label: Vainakh Tower Architecture
defn: the stone residential and battle towers of the Chechens and Ingush in the North Caucasus (11th–18th century), the battle towers with stepped pyramidal roofs: Vovnushki, Erzi, Nikaroy.
aliases: Vainakh towers; Ingush towers; Chechen towers

label: Spanish Vernacular Architecture
defn: the traditional rural houses of Spain in their regional types and materials: the Catalan masia, the Cantabrian casona and casa montañesa, the Basque and Navarrese casa torre and caserío.
aliases: arquitectura popular española; Spanish rural architecture

label: Italian Vernacular Architecture
defn: the traditional rural building of Italy and its islands in local stone and earth: the corbelled dry-stone trulli of Apulia, the domed dammusi of Pantelleria.
aliases: architettura rurale; architettura spontanea; Italian rural architecture

label: American Vernacular Architecture
defn: the folk and vernacular house types of the United States, classified by plan and massing rather than by style: the shotgun house, the I-house, the upright-and-wing house, the New England connected farm, the Charleston single house.
aliases: American folk architecture; vernacular architecture of the United States; American folk house

label: Nordic Log Architecture
defn: the notched solid-log building tradition of Scandinavia and Finland for houses, farm buildings and churches: Norwegian lofts and stabbur, Swedish timmerhus, Finnish hirsitalo farmhouses.
aliases: log architecture; laft; lafteverk; timmerhus; hirsitalo; Scandinavian log building

label: Swiss Farmhouse Architecture
defn: the traditional timber farmhouses of Switzerland in their regional types, the vernacular source of the chalet: the Frutighaus of the Bernese Oberland, the Bernese Mittelland house, the Appenzell house.
aliases: Schweizer Bauernhaus; Swiss chalet (vernacular); Bernese farmhouse

label: French Vernacular Architecture
defn: the traditional rural houses of France in their regional types: the longère of Brittany and Normandy, the mas of Provence, the Basque etxe.

label: Cycladic Architecture
defn: the whitewashed cubic stone houses, chapels and windmills of the Cyclades, flat-roofed and set in dense hill villages: Oia (Santorini), Chora (Mykonos), Kastro (Sifnos).

label: Chattel House
defn: the small movable timber house of Barbados, built on loose stone blocks without nails so tenants could dismantle it, with gabled roof and fretwork trim: Tyrol Cot Heritage Village.

label: Queenslander
defn: the timber house of Queensland raised on stumps, with corrugated-iron roof and deep verandas, built from the 1840s to today: workers' cottages and high-set houses of Brisbane's inner suburbs.

label: Persian Garden
defn: The walled garden of Iran laid out as a chahar bagh, four plots divided by water channels around a pavilion, from Achaemenid Pasargadae to the Safavid and Qajar gardens (UNESCO 2011): Pasargadae, Bagh-e Fin, Kashan, Eram Garden, Shiraz, Shazdeh Garden, Mahan.

label: Mughal Garden
defn: The gardens of the Mughal emperors in South Asia, 16th–18th century, built on the chahar bagh with terraces, cascades and tomb or pleasure pavilions: Humayun's Tomb garden, Taj Mahal charbagh, Shalimar Bagh, Srinagar, Shalimar Gardens, Lahore.

label: Chinese Garden
defn: The Chinese classical garden of rocks, water, pavilions and planting composed as a landscape in miniature, in its imperial and scholar's (literati) forms: Humble Administrator's Garden, Lingering Garden, Summer Palace, Yu Garden.
aliases: Chinese classical garden;scholar's garden;Chinese scholar garden;yuanlin

label: Japanese Garden
defn: The Japanese garden tradition from the Heian pond garden through the Zen dry landscape and the tea garden to the Edo stroll garden: Ryōan-ji rock garden, Saihō-ji moss garden, Katsura Imperial Villa, Kenroku-en.

label: Italian Renaissance Garden
defn: The terraced villa garden of 15th–16th-century Italy, ordered by axis and geometry with fountains, grottoes, statuary and giochi d'acqua: Villa d'Este, Tivoli, Boboli Gardens, Villa Lante, Bagnaia, Sacro Bosco, Bomarzo.

label: French Formal Garden
defn: The garden à la française of 17th-century France, a geometric composition of parterres, basins and long axes ordered from the château, perfected by André Le Nôtre: Vaux-le-Vicomte, Gardens of Versailles, Chantilly, Tuileries.
aliases: garden à la française;jardin à la française;French garden;formal garden

label: English Landscape Garden
defn: The informal 'natural' landscape park of 18th-century Britain, with lawns, serpentine lakes, belts of trees and temples composed as pictures, and its picturesque and international offshoots: Stourhead, Stowe, Blenheim Park, Wörlitz Park.
aliases: English garden;English landscape park;jardin à l'anglaise;landscape garden

label: Bonsai
defn: the Japanese art of the trained miniature tree in a container, shaped by pruning and wiring into named styles and size classes and shown in alcove display: Ōmiya Bonsai Village, the Kokufu-ten exhibition, saikei tray landscapes.

label: Penjing
defn: the Chinese art of miniature trees and landscapes in containers (from the Tang dynasty), in tree, rock-landscape and water-and-land forms and regional schools, precursor of bonsai: Lingnan, Shanghai, Yangzhou, Suzhou and Sichuan penjing.

label: Hòn Non Bộ
defn: the Vietnamese art of miniature rock landscapes of islands and mountains set in water with plants, viewed from all sides (from the 10th century).
aliases: hon non bo; Vietnamese miniature landscape

label: Ikebana
defn: the Japanese art of flower arrangement (kadō), from Buddhist altar offerings to the schools that codified its forms: Ikenobō rikka and shōka, Ohara moribana, Sōgetsu free style.
aliases: kadō; way of the flower; Japanese flower arrangement

label: Bhimbetka Rock Paintings
defn: Painted rock shelters of the Vindhyan hills from the Mesolithic to the historical period (UNESCO 2003): hunting scenes, dancers, Zoo Rock.

label: Petroglyphs of the Mongolian Altai
defn: The rock carvings and paintings of the Mongolian Altai (UNESCO 2011), from about 11,000 years ago to the Turkic period: Tsagaan Salaa, Upper Tsagaan Gol, Aral Tolgoi.
aliases: Petroglyphic Complexes of the Mongolian Altai

label: Tamgaly Petroglyphs
defn: The Bronze Age to medieval rock carvings of Tamgaly and the Semirechye (UNESCO 2004), with sun-headed figures and sacrificial scenes: sun-headed deities, bull and chariot scenes.

label: Maros-Pangkep Cave Art
defn: Painted and stencilled rock art of the limestone karst of South Sulawesi, among the oldest figurative art known (45,000+ years): Leang Tedongnge warty pig, Leang Bulu' Sipong 4 hunting scene, hand stencils.

label: Sangkulirang-Mangkalihat Rock Art
defn: Hand stencils and animal paintings of the limestone caves of East Kalimantan and of Niah in Sarawak: Lubang Jeriji Saléh banteng, Niah Painted Cave.

label: Zuojiang Huashan Rock Art
defn: Red-ochre rock paintings of the Luo Yue people on cliffs along the Zuojiang river in Guangxi (5th c. BCE–2nd c. CE), with figures and bronze drums (UNESCO 2016).

label: Bangudae Petroglyphs
defn: Neolithic and Bronze Age petroglyphs on the Daegok stream in Ulsan, with whales, hunters and boats, and the nearby Cheonjeon-ri carvings (UNESCO 2025).

label: Fugoppe Cave
defn: Incised figures and signs in the Fugoppe cave in Hokkaido (Epi-Jōmon) and the related Temiya cave carvings.

label: Helan Mountains Petroglyphs
